source_assistant: Speculative decoding uses a draft model to propose tokens and a target model to verify them; speedup depends on acceptance rate and verification cost.
corrected_answer:
Contrast: speculative decoding vs. plain autoregressive decoding.

Assumptions stated up front: single target model served on GPU, batch size small enough that decode is memory-bandwidth bound (this is the regime where the technique pays), greedy or low-temperature sampling, draft and target share a tokenizer. Numbers below are quantities to measure on your own stack, not vendor-published facts.

Baseline (naive) mechanism. Autoregressive decode emits one token per forward pass. Each pass must stream the full weight set (and the KV cache slice) from HBM, so per-token latency is approximately (bytes_read / achievable_HBM_bandwidth), independent of how much arithmetic the layer does. Arithmetic intensity is ~1 token of work per weight read, so the GPU sits far below peak FLOPs.

Concrete mechanism of speculative decoding. A cheap draft (small model, n-gram/prompt-lookup table, or Medusa/EAGLE-style extra heads) proposes gamma candidate tokens autoregressively. The target model then runs ONE forward pass over all gamma+1 positions in parallel, because the candidate prefix is known. A rejection-sampling verification step walks the candidates left to right: candidate i is accepted with probability min(1, p_target(x_i)/p_draft(x_i)); on the first rejection the token is resampled from the normalized residual distribution (p_target - p_draft)_+ and all later candidates are discarded. This acceptance rule is what makes the output distribution provably identical to sampling from the target model alone -- the speedup is free of quality loss, which is the central difference from lossy alternatives such as quantizing or swapping in the small model outright.

The economics. Naive decode: 1 token per target pass. Speculative: E[accepted]+1 tokens per target pass, where for acceptance rate alpha and block gamma, E[accepted] = (1-alpha^(gamma+1))/(1-alpha) - 1. Net speedup = that expected yield divided by (1 + gamma*C_draft/C_target + C_verify/C_target).

Boundary condition (where the contrast inverts). Once the target model's decode step is compute-bound rather than bandwidth-bound -- large continuous batches, long-context attention dominating, or high tensor-parallel degree -- verifying gamma+1 positions costs roughly gamma+1 times a single position instead of being nearly free. At that point the draft overhead is pure loss and speculative decoding is SLOWER than the naive path. The crossover is measurable: sweep batch size and record tokens/s with and without speculation; the batch size where the curves cross is your cutoff, and a production serving stack should disable speculation above it rather than assume it always helps.

Evidence I would require before claiming a win: measured acceptance rate alpha per workload, tokens/s and p50/p99 TTFT+TPOT at the target batch size for both paths, and a distribution-equivalence check (identical outputs under a fixed seed for greedy). Rollback gate: revert to naive decode if p99 latency regresses at any batch size in the served range, or if alpha falls below the break-even implied by the formula above.

source_user: Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with speculative decoding. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Speculative decoding uses a draft model to propose tokens and a target model to verify them; speedup depends on acceptance rate and verification cost.
corrected_answer:
Two failure modes / trade-offs of speculative decoding, with mechanism and boundary conditions.

Assumptions: target model served with continuous batching, draft is a smaller model or a lightweight head, tokenizers aligned. Everything numeric below is a quantity to measure on your stack.

Failure mode 1 -- negative speedup under batching (compute-bound inversion). Mechanism: speculative decoding trades a bandwidth-bound step for a compute-bound one. At batch size 1 the target forward pass is dominated by streaming weights from HBM, so verifying gamma+1 positions in one pass costs almost the same as verifying one -- the extra tokens are nearly free. As the server fills up, the decode step becomes GEMM-bound and verification cost grows roughly linearly in gamma+1, while the draft model's gamma sequential passes are added on top. Boundary condition: there is a batch size B* above which total tokens/s with speculation is lower than without. B* is not a constant -- it moves with sequence length, TP degree, and draft size. Falsifiable claim: sweep batch size 1..max and plot tokens/s for both paths; if the curves never cross in your served range, this failure mode does not apply to you. Operationally you want a scheduler that can turn speculation off per-step when the running batch exceeds B*, not a static config flag.

Failure mode 2 -- acceptance-rate collapse on distribution shift, and the wasted-work tail. Mechanism: expected accepted tokens per block is (1-alpha^(gamma+1))/(1-alpha) - 1, which is superlinearly sensitive to alpha. A draft trained or tuned on general chat data will see alpha drop sharply on out-of-distribution traffic -- code, non-English, long structured JSON, RAG contexts with unusual tokens, or high sampling temperature (raising temperature flattens p_target and lowers the min(1, p_t/p_d) ratio). When alpha falls, every rejected candidate is draft compute plus verification compute that produced nothing, so you pay strictly more than the naive path per emitted token. Boundary condition: break-even alpha is the value where E[accepted]+1 equals the per-step overhead ratio 1 + gamma*C_draft/C_target; below it, disable. Secondary trade-off: gamma itself has an optimum -- larger gamma raises the ceiling but wastes more on rejection, so tail latency variance grows even when mean latency improves. That matters for SLOs expressed as p99 inter-token latency, which can regress while mean tokens/s improves.

Two more costs worth naming honestly: the draft model occupies HBM that would otherwise hold KV cache (reducing max concurrency), and any tokenizer or vocabulary mismatch between draft and target breaks the acceptance math outright rather than merely degrading it.

Evidence required: per-route acceptance rate histograms, tokens/s and p50/p99 TPOT with and without speculation at production batch sizes, HBM occupancy delta and resulting max-concurrency delta, and a seeded output-equivalence test proving verification is implemented correctly. Rollback gate: disable speculation if measured alpha drops below break-even for more than a short window, or if p99 TPOT regresses, even if mean throughput improved.

How speculative decoding interacts with latency, throughput, and memory.

Assumptions: single-node GPU serving, continuous batching, draft and target share a tokenizer, and the verification step implements the standard rejection-sampling rule so output distribution is unchanged. All thresholds below are to be measured, not assumed.

Latency. This is where the technique is designed to win. Per-token decode latency in the small-batch regime is bounded by weight streaming: t_step ~= bytes_read / effective_HBM_bandwidth. Speculative decoding does not make that step cheaper; it amortizes it over multiple accepted tokens. Concrete mechanism: the draft proposes gamma tokens, the target verifies all gamma+1 positions in a single forward pass because the candidate prefix is already known, and E[accepted]+1 = (1-alpha^(gamma+1))/(1-alpha) tokens are emitted per target pass. So inter-token latency (TPOT) falls by roughly that factor minus draft overhead. Note TTFT is essentially unaffected -- prefill is already parallel and compute-bound, so do not promise TTFT improvements. Also note the latency distribution gets lumpier: tokens arrive in accepted bursts, so p99 inter-token gaps can widen even as the mean falls, which matters if your SLO is per-token rather than per-response.

Throughput. The interaction is the opposite sign at scale. Aggregate tokens/s at high concurrency is compute-bound, and speculation adds work: gamma sequential draft passes plus a verification pass over gamma+1 positions, of which the rejected suffix is discarded. Boundary condition: above a measurable batch size B*, speculation reduces system throughput. The correct framing is that speculative decoding converts spare FLOPs into lower latency; if you have no spare FLOPs, there is nothing to convert. A serving stack should therefore treat speculation as a latency knob gated on current batch occupancy, not a global on/off.

Memory. Two distinct pressures. (1) Draft weights permanently occupy HBM, directly reducing the pool available for KV cache and therefore max concurrent sequences -- a 1B draft beside a 70B target in FP16 is ~2 GB, which at typical per-sequence KV footprints can cost a meaningful number of slots. Head-based drafts (Medusa/EAGLE) are much cheaper here, which is their main argument. (2) Verification needs KV entries for gamma+1 speculative positions per sequence, and rejected positions must be rolled back. If the cache manager cannot cheaply truncate, you either over-allocate blocks or pay a copy per rejection. With paged KV this is usually a block-index rollback and is cheap, but it is a real correctness surface: a rollback bug silently corrupts context rather than crashing.

Falsifiable claims and evidence: measure alpha per route; measure p50/p99 TPOT and tokens/s with speculation on and off across the full served batch range to locate B*; measure HBM occupancy and resulting max-concurrency delta; run seeded greedy equivalence tests to prove verification and KV rollback are correct. Rollback gate: disable speculation if p99 TPOT regresses, if throughput at production concurrency drops, or if max concurrency falls enough to raise queueing delay above the SLO -- queueing regressions routinely erase decode-side wins.
